text: This is a warehouse on the edge of Fort Wayne, Indiana. Two roofs on one building. The older half is a metal building with an exposed-fastener roof: steel panels screwed straight through to the purlins, thousands of screws, each one sealed by a small rubber washer. The newer half is a flat addition with a white single-ply membrane, a PVC or TPO sheet, heat-welded at the seams, with rooftop units on curbs, two drains, a hatch and a parapet. Both are new today. Watch what fifteen years does to them, and what a roofer can do about it.

Years one to five. Every sunny day the roofs heat up and every night they cool down. A dark roof in summer can reach a hundred and fifty degrees; in an Indiana January the same steel sits below zero. Steel grows and shrinks with that. On a forty-foot panel, that is roughly a quarter inch over a summer day and about half an inch across the year. A standing-seam roof rides that movement on sliding clips. Most exposed-fastener roofs have no allowance for it. The panel pulls against the screws, twice a day, and the holes slowly wallow out. The rubber washers bake, dry, and crack. On the membrane side, the sun's ultraviolet works on the top layer, and the white dulls under dirt. The roof is still dry. Nothing has failed yet.

Here is one summer day on that metal roof. The air peaks near ninety. The panel peaks far higher, then drops back to the air temperature at night. The panel moves with it. Over the years that is thousands of cycles, each one working the screw in its hole.

Years five to fifteen. Plain zinc-plated screw heads often rust before the panel does; long-life fasteners hold up better. Then the rust spreads to the panel at the end laps and around the holes where the washers have failed, and the backed-out screws stand proud with daylight under them. On the flat roof, the slope was never perfect, and the deck has deflected a little. Water now sits in the low spots for days after a rain. Roofers call it ponding when it is still there forty-eight hours later. A drain strainer clogs with leaves and a plastic bag. The membrane under the pond grows algae, and the sun keeps cooking the rest.

Then the small failures. A welded seam that was never fully bonded opens into a fishmouth. A service tech drops a screw and steps on it; another sets a sharp tool down on hot membrane. The flashing at the rooftop-unit curb, cut and sealed by hand, cracks at the corners. Every one of those is a hole, and some of them are under water.
Inside, the first sign is a brown ring on a ceiling tile or a drip off the deck, usually nowhere near the hole. Water runs along the deck ribs before it finds a way down.

Here is the flat roof in cutaway. From the top: the membrane, a cover board, two layers of foam insulation, the steel deck, the bar joist. Water through a seam does not drip straight down. It soaks into the insulation and spreads, sometimes well beyond the hole. Wet insulation loses much of its insulating value, and it stays wet, because the membrane that let the water in also keeps it from drying. The steel deck underneath rusts from the top, where no one can see it. By the time the ceiling stains, the roof may have been wet for a long time.

At this point the owner has choices: patch it, lay a new roof over it, restore it with a coating, or tear it all off and start over. Whether a coating is even an option depends first on how much of the roof is wet, and then on the deck, the adhesion, and the drainage.

A restoration starts with a moisture survey: an infrared scan after sunset, when wet insulation holds heat longer than dry, confirmed with core cuts. Wet areas are cut out and replaced with dry insulation and new membrane, and the clogged drains are cleared. Then the whole roof is power washed. On the metal side, loose screws are tightened or replaced, and a larger screw goes into any hole that has worn out. Rust is wire-brushed and primed with a rust-inhibiting primer. Then the screw heads are sealed over, and the laps, seams and penetrations are reinforced, often with fabric embedded in sealant.

Then the coating: a fluid-applied silicone or acrylic, sprayed or rolled, in one or two coats depending on the product, to a thickness the manufacturer specifies. Typically twenty to forty thousandths of an inch dry, depending on the warranty, ten to twenty years. Silicone stays flexible and tolerates standing water. Acrylic costs less but needs a dry roof and warm weather to cure. Both turn an old roof bright white again.

Why white? A new white roof reflects about eighty percent of the sunlight that hits it. A dark roof reflects five to twenty. After three years of dirt, a white roof typically still reflects fifty-five to sixty-five percent, and the rating labs test both numbers. On a sunny summer afternoon, the Department of Energy says, a conventional roof can reach a hundred and fifty degrees, and a cool roof stays about fifty degrees cooler. Cooler means less thermal movement, less stress on the screws and the seams, and lower air conditioning bills. The savings depend on climate. Indiana winters give some of it back.

What a coating cannot do. It cannot dry out wet insulation. It cannot fix a rusted-through deck or a rotten one. It cannot add slope where water ponds. Those get repaired first, or the roof gets replaced. Done right, a restoration typically carries a ten to twenty year warranty, usually for well under the cost of a tear-off, and a maintained roof can be coated again. A roof does not die of one big thing. It dies of thousands of sunny days and nobody checking the screws.
